newsitem.title: UK: Oil rally leaves other raw materials to flounder.
newsitem.headline: Oil rally leaves other raw materials to flounder.

text.p: Most commodities except oil, on which the price set a new post-Gulf War record, were sunk in an unseasonal torpor on Monday.

Gold was hardly changed and the industrial metals eased after an attempt to rally last week by copper fizzled out -- even though end-user demand for raw materials should be picking up at this time of year.

Speculative money showed scant interest in the commodity sector away from crude oil where the nearby London futures contract for the benchmark Brent Blend hit $2.75 per barrel, the highest price since the 1991 Gulf War.
Renewed faction fighting among Iraqi Kurds prompted the latest gain in oil prices, already supported by strong demand for heating fuel ahead of the northern winter.

Copper prices eased in subdued trading after a rally last week failed to break strong technical resistance at $1,970 per tonne and were around $1,935 late in the London Metal Exchange (LME) Monday afternoon.

Britain's Guardian newspaper reported that back in June U.S. investment bank Goldman Sachs had been given the highly sensitive assignment of unwinding a huge stockpile of copper that had been built up by Sumitomo Corp of Japan.

It also suggested that this might bring Goldman into conflict with regulatory agencies that are investigating alleged maverick deals by Yasuo Hamanaka, the Sumitomo trader who was alleged to have built the hoard and then lost $2.6 billion.

"Since the beginning of our assignment for our client Sumitomo Corporation we have worked closely with regulators on both sides of the Atlantic. We are not in conflict with any authority," David Woods, Goldman Sachs International director of European Media Relations, said in a news release.
Aluminium held above recent 2 1/2-year lows and traded just above $1,325 per tonne but just easier from Friday.
Speculation that producers might reach a new accord to curb excess aluminium output abated.

Government spokesmen in Australia, Canada and Norway all said they were unaware of any plans to renew a 1994 Memorandum of Understanding which expired earlier this year. But the producers may cooperate on providing statistics.
Gold ended in London at $381.40/$381.90 per ounce after $381.10/$381.60 on Friday. Dealers said it was range trading in $380-$382 band.
Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) December wheat futures were also little changed just above $4.25 per bushel whilst coffee and cocoa were slightly easier.
